label: Thm:Lifting
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:Lifting}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops of genus $g$ and $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution.  Let $K$ be an algebraically closed nonarchimedean field of odd residue characteristic or characteristic zero, let $C$ be a bielliptic curve of genus $g$ over $K$, and $f \colon \widetilde{C} \to C$ an \'{e}tale double cover that specializes to $\pi$.  Then every divisor class in $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ lifts to a divisor class in $V^r (C,f)$.

label: Cor:Class
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor:Class}
Let $r \geq 2$.  For a general \'{e}tale double cover $[f \colon C] \to \widetilde{C} \in \mathcal{R}_{B,g,0}$, one has the following equality of cohomology classes:
\[
[ V^r (C,f) ] = 2 \cdot \frac{\Theta^{r+1}}{(r+1)!}.
\]

label: Lem:Irreducible
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Irreducible}
If $g \geq 3$, $a \leq g-2$, and $Z_a$ is nonempty, then $Z_a$ is irreducible of dimension $g-1-a$.  When $g(C_1) = 1$, the variety $Z_{g-1}$ consists of two points.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is shown in \cite[Lemma~5.3]{Horing} in all cases except when $g(C_1) = 1$ and $a \geq g-2$.  When $g(C_1) = 1$, the map $p_1 \colon C_1 \to E$ is an isogeny of degree 2, hence $\mathrm{Nm}_{p_1}$ has kernel of order 2.  It follows immediately that
\[
Z_{g-1} = \{ ([D_1], 0) \mid \mathrm{Nm}_{p_1} (D_1) \sim \delta \}
\]
consists of 2 points.

We now show that, if $g(C_1)=1$, then $Z_{g-2}$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{C}$.  Since $\widetilde{C}$ is an irreducible curve, the result will follow.  Let $\delta' \in \mathrm{Nm}_{p_1}^{-1} (\delta)$.  Consider the map $k \colon \widetilde{C} \to W^0_{g-2} (C_1) \times W^0_1 (C_2)$ given by
\[
k(x) = ( \delta' - \mathrm{Nm}_{f_1} (x), \mathrm{Nm}_{f_2} (x)) .
\]
Note that, since $g \geq 3$, we have $g-2 \geq 1$, and since $g(C_1)=1$, every divisor class of degree $g-2$ on $C_1$ is effective.  Hence, the image of $k$ is contained in $Z_{g-2}$.  Moreover, one has the commutative diagram:
\[
\xymatrix {
\widetilde{C} \ar[r]^{k} \ar[rd]_{f_1} & Z_{g-2} \ar[d] \\
& C_2 
 }
\]
where the left arrow is an \'{e}tale double cover by construction and the right arrow is an \'{e}tale double cover because $\mathrm{Nm}_{p_1}$ has kernel of order 2.  It follows that $k$ must be an isomorphism.

label: Lem:Simple
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: Cor:Irreducible
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor:Irreducible}
If $1 \leq a \leq g-2$ and $Y_a$ is nonempty, then it is irreducible of dimension $g-1-a$.  When $g(C_1) = 1$, $Y_{g-1}$ consists of two points.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $a \leq g-2$, $Z_a$ is irreducible by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Irreducible}, hence its image $Y_a$ is irreducible as well.  When $a=0$, by \cite[Proposition~5.2.1]{Debarre}, we have $\mathrm{dim} (Y_a) = g-2$, hence the condition $a \geq 1$ in the statement above.  For the remaining statements, it suffices to prove that the map from $Z_a$ to $Y_a$ is generically injective.  If $a \geq 1$, then for a general element $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_a$, we have $[D_2]$ is $p_2$-simple and $h^0 (C_1,D_1) = a$.  Hence, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Simple}, we have
\[
h^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2) \leq 2h^0 (C_1, D_1) - a = h^0 (C_1,D_1).
\]
In other words, every section of $f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2$ is of the form $f_1^* s_1 + f_2^* s_2$ for $s_1 \in H^0 (C_1,D_1)$ and $s_2$ the unique element of $H^0 (C_2,D_2)$.  Thus, the divisor classes $[D_1], [D_2]$ are determined by $[f_1^*D_1 + f_2^* D_2]$, hence the map is generically injective.

label: Lem:PBNContains
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:PBNContains}
We have $Y_{r+1} \subseteq V^r (C,f)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_{r+1}$.  Since $h^0 (C_2 , D_2 ) \geq 1$ and pullback of sections is injective, we have the following inclusions:
\[
H^0 (C_1, D_1) \hookrightarrow H^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1) \hookrightarrow H^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2).
\]
Hence,
\[
h^0 (C_1 , D_1) \leq h^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2).
\]
Since $\deg (D_1) = g(C_1)+r$, by Riemann-Roch we have $h^0 (C_1 , D_1 ) \geq r+1$.  It follows that $h^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2) \geq r+1$, hence $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in V^r (C,f)$.
head: environment

label: Lem:Containment
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Containment}
Let $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_a$.  If $[D_1]$ is not $p_1$-simple, then $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in Y_a \cap Y_{a-2}$.  Similarly, if $[D_2]$ is not $p_2$-simple, then $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in Y_a \cap Y_{a+2}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The divisor class $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2]$ is in $Y_a$ by definition.  We consider the case where $[D_1]$ is not $p_1$-simple.  The case where $[D_2]$ is not $p_2$-simple follows by a similar argument.  If $[D_1]$ is not $p_1$-simple, then by definition, there exists a point $x \in E$ such that $D_1 - p_1^* (x)$ is equivalent to an effective divisor $A$.  It follows that
\[
f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2 \sim (f_1^* A + f_1^* p_1^* x) + f_2^* D_2 = f_1^* A + (f_2^* p_2^* x + f_2^* D_2) .
\]
The divisor class on the righthand side is in $Y_{a-2}$, and the result follows.
head: environment

label: Cor:WhenContains
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor:WhenContains}
If $a \geq 1$, then $Y_{a+2} \subseteq Y_a$.  Moreover, if $g(C_1)=1$, for $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_a$, one has $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in Y_{a+2}$ if and only if $[D_2]$ is not $p_2$-simple.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_{a+2}$.  Since $\deg (D_1) = g(C_1)+1+a \geq g(C_1)+2$, by Riemann-Roch we have $h^0 (C_1 , D_1 ) \geq 3$.  It follows that, for any effective divisor $D'$ of degree 2 on $C_1$, $D_1 - D'$ is equivalent to an effective divisor.  In particular, for any point $x \in E$, $D_1 - p_1^* (x)$ is equivalent to an effective divisor.  In other words, $[D_1]$ is not $p_1$-simple, so by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Containment}, we have $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in Y_a$.  Since $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_{a+2}$ is arbitrary, we see that $Y_{a+2} \subseteq Y_a$.

Now, let $g(C_1) = 1$ and let $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_a$.  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Containment}, if $[D_2]$ is not $p_2$-simple, then $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in Y_{a+2}$.  If $[D_2]$ is $p_2$-simple, then by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Simple}, we have
\[
h^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2) \leq 2h^0 (C_1, D_1) - a = a.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:PBNContains}, however, if $f_1^* [D_1] + f_2^* [D_2] \in Y_{a+2}$, then $h^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2) \geq a+2$, a contradiction.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g(C_1)=1$.  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:PBNContains}, we have $Y_{r+1} \subseteq V^r (C,f)$.  We now prove the reverse containment.

Let $[D] \in V^r (C,f)$.  If $r$ is odd, then by \cite[Proposition~5.2.1]{Debarre}, we have $[D] \in Y_0$.  Similarly, if $r$ is even, then by \cite[Corollary~5.7]{Horing}, we have $[D] \in Y_3$.  Let $a$ be the maximum integer such that $[D] \in Y_a$.  Then there exists $([D_1],[D_2]) \in Z_a$ such that $D \sim f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2$.  If $[D_2]$ is not $p_2$-simple, then by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Containment}, we have $[D] = [f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2] \in Y_{a+2}$, contradicting the maximality of $a$.  It follows that $[D_2]$ is $p_2$-simple, hence by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Simple}, we have
\[
h^0 (\widetilde{C}, D) = h^0 (\widetilde{C}, f_1^* D_1 + f_2^* D_2) \leq 2h^0 (C_1, D_1) - a.
\]
By Riemann-Roch, the expression on the right is at most 2 if $a=0$ and equal to $a$ if $a \geq 1$.  Since $r \geq 2$ and $[D] \in V^r (C,f)$, it follows that $a \geq r+1$.  By Corollary~\ref{Cor:WhenContains}, we then have $[D] \in Y_{r+1}$.
head: environment

label: Lem:Intersection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Intersection}
Let $g(C_1) = 1$.  For $r \geq 2$, there exists an integer $m_r \geq 2$ such that
\[
[ V^r (C,f) ] =  m_r \cdot \frac{\Theta^{r+1}}{(r+1)!} .
\]
Moreover, the intersection of $V^r (C,f)$ with $g-r-2$ general translates of $V^1 (C,f)$ consists of at least 
\[
2 \cdot \frac{(g-1)!}{(r+1)!}
\]
distinct points.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Theorem~4.1(i)]{Debarre}, if $X$ is a hyperelliptic curve of genus $g-1$, then the Jacobian $\operatorname{Jac} (X)$ is contained in the closure of $\mathcal{R}_{B,g,0}$ in the moduli space of abelian varieties.  A general hyperelliptic curve has the property that the cohomology class of every subvariety of its Jacobian is an integral multiple of the minimal class $\frac{\Theta^k}{k!}$.  Thus, there exists an integer $m_r$ such that
\[
[ Y_{r+1} ] = m_r \cdot \frac{\Theta^{r+1}}{(r+1)!}.
\]
Similarly, there exists an integer $n_r$ such that the class of the reduced scheme $Y_{r+1}^{\mathrm{red}}$ is equal to $m_r \cdot \frac{\Theta^{r+1}}{(r+1)!}$.  It suffices to show that $m_r$ and $n_r$ are both at least 2.  By Corollary~\ref{Cor:Irreducible}, $Y_{g-1}$ consists of two distinct points, so the statement hold when $r+1 = g-1$.   When $r+1 \leq g-2$, the assumption that $r \geq 2$ implies that $g \geq 5$.  It therefore suffices to show that, for $g \geq 5$ and $d$ in the range $1 \leq d \leq g-2$, the Prym variety $\mathrm{Prym}(C,f)$ of a general cover $[f \colon \widetilde{C} \to C] \in \mathcal{R}_{B,g,0}$ does not contain a closed subscheme $X$ of dimension $d$ with $[X] = \frac{\Theta^{g-1-d}}{(g-1-d)!}$.

We prove this by induction on $d$.  The base case, where $d=1$, follows from the Matsusaka-Ran criterion \cite[Theorem~3]{Ran} because for a general cover $[f \colon \widetilde{C} \to C] \in \mathcal{R}_{B,g,0}$, the Prym variety $\mathrm{Prym}(C,f)$ is not a Jacobian.  For the inductive step, let $[f \colon \widetilde{D} \to D] \in \mathcal{R}_{B,g-1,0}$.  Let $E$ be a curve of genus 1, let $C_0$ be the 2-component curve obtained by identifying a point $p \in D$ with a point $q \in E$, and let $\widetilde{C}_0$ be the 3-component curve obtained by identifying each of the 2 preimage points of $p$ in $\widetilde{D}$ with the point $q$ in two separate copies of $E$.  The admissible cover $[g \colon \widetilde{C}_0 \to C_0]$ is contained in the closure of $\mathcal{R}_{B,g,0}$ in the moduli space $\overline{\mathcal{R}}_g$.  The Prym variety of this cover is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Prym}(D,f) \times \operatorname{Jac}(E)$.  Thus, if $X$ is a closed subscheme of this Prym variety with $[X] = \frac{\Theta^{g-1-d}}{(g-1-d)!}$, then the intersection of $X$ with $\mathrm{Prym}(D,f) \times \{ 0 \}$ has class $\frac{\Theta^{g-1-d}}{(g-1-d)!}$ as well.  By our induction hypothesis, if $[f \colon \widetilde{D} \to D]$ is sufficiently general, then $\mathrm{Prym}(D,f)$ does not contain a closed subscheme with this class, hence $\mathrm{Prym} (C_0,g)$ cannot contain such a closed subscheme either.

body_md:

label: Thm:PBNBielliptic
title: Theorem
body_md:
\cite[Theorem~6.8]{PBN}
\label{Thm:PBNBielliptic}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops and $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution.  If $r \geq 2$, then
\[
V^r (\Gamma,\pi) = \bigcup T(Q),
\]
where the union is over all lingering words of length $g-1$ in the Coxeter group $I_2 (r+1)$ that contain one of the two reduced subwords of maximal length $r+1$.

In the special case where $r=2$, the statement holds for every loop of loops $\Gamma$, regardless of edge lengths.

label: Thm:Zonotope
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:Zonotope}
The poset $P(r+1,n)$ is the face lattice of a zonotope.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix positive integers $r$ and $n$ with $r+1 \leq n$.  There exists an oriented matroid on $E=[n]$ of rank $n-r$, called the \emph{alternating matroid}, with signed circuits defined as follows.   For every subset $C \subseteq E$ of size $\vert C \vert = r+1$, write $C = \{ c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_{r+1} \}$ with $c_i < c_{i+1}$ for all $i$.  Then $(C^+, C^-)$ is a signed circuit of the alternating matroid, where $C^+ = \{ c_1, c_3, c_5, \ldots \}$ and $C^- = \{ c_2 , c_4, c_6 , \ldots \}$.  The set of signed vectors of the alternating matroid are the signed sets $V=(V^+,V^-)$ such that there exists a signed circuit $C=(C^+,C^-)$ with $C^+ \subseteq V^+$ and $C^- \subseteq V^-$.  Given two signed vectors $V_1 = (V_1^+ , V_1^-), V_2 = (V_2^+ , V_2^-)$, we have $V_1 \leq V_2$ if and only if $V_1^+ \subseteq V_2^+$ and $V_1^- \subseteq V_2^-)$.

Given a signed vector $V = (V^+ , V^-)$ in the alternating matroid, we define a lingering word $Q = s_1 \cdots s_n$ by
\[
s_i = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
r_0 & \text{if } i \in V^+ \\
r_1 & \text{if } i \in V^- \\
\epsilon &\text{otherwise. }
\end{array} \right.
\]
This defines an order-reversing bijection from the lattice of vectors of the alternating matroid to $P(r+1,n)$.

By \cite[Corollary~8.2.10]{OrientedMatroids}, the alternating matroid is realizable.  An oriented matroid is realizable if and only if its dual matroid is realizable.  Thus, there exists a set of vectors $\vec{x}_1 , \ldots , \vec{x}_n \in \mathbb{R}^{n-r}$ whose lattice of covectors is anti-isomorphic to $P(r+1,n)$.  The result then follows from Proposition~\ref{Prop:ZonotopeMatroid}.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Theorem~\ref{Thm:PBNBielliptic} shows that $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ is a union of tori, and Lemma~\ref{Lem:Contains} shows that the intersection lattice of these tori is $P(r+1,g-1)$.  The result then follows from Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zonotope}.
head: environment

label: Ex:LowDim
title: Example
body_md:
\label{Ex:LowDim}
A consequence of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zonotope} is that the order complex of $P(r+1,g-1)$ is homeomorphic to a sphere of dimension $g-r-2$.  Thus, when $g-r-2=0$, the tropical Prym-Brill-Noether variety $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ consists of 2 points.  When $g-r-2=1$, the poset $P(r+1,g-1)$ is the face poset of a graph with $2g-2$ vertices and $2g-2$ edges, arranged in a cycle.  Thus, in this case, the Prym-Brill-Noether variety $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ is itself a loop of loops of genus $2g-1$.  One can check that it is isomorphic to the metric graph obtained from $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ by contracting the edge from $w_{i-1}$ to $v_i$ for all $i$.  (The Prym-Brill-Noether variety of the cover $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ is independent of the lengths of these edges, so one cannot expect it to be isomorphic to $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ itself.)  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Irreducible}, this is analogous to the classical case.  Specifically, when $g(C_1)=1$ and $g-r-2=0$, the classical Prym-Brill-Noether variety $V^r (C,f)$ consists of 2 points, and when $g-r-2=1$, the classical Prym-Brill-Noether variety is isomorphic to $\widetilde{C}$.

label: Def:VA
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:VA}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops, let $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution, and let $Q = s_1 \cdots s_{g-1} \in P(r+1,g-1)$ be a word with $\# \{ j \mid s_j = \epsilon \} = g-2-r$.  A divisor $[D] \in T(Q)$ is \emph{vertex avoiding} if, for all $i$ such that $s_i = \epsilon$, the chip of the orientable representative of $[D]$ on the $i$th loop is neither $v_i$ nor $w_i$.
head: environment

label: Lem:TropIntersection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:TropIntersection}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops and $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution.  For $r \geq 2$, there exist divisors $D_1 , \ldots , D_{g-2-r} \in P^r (\Gamma,\pi) - P^1 (\Gamma,\pi)$ such that
\[
X = \bigcap_{i=1}^{g-2-r} [V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + D_i ] \cap V^r (\Gamma,\pi)
\]
is finite and
\[
\# X = 2 \cdot \frac{(g-1)!}{(r+1)!}.
\]
Moreover, if $[D] \in V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ is vertex avoiding, then the divisors $D_i$ can be chosen to so that $[D] \in X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{Thm:PBNBielliptic}, $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ is a union of tori $T(Q)$ corresponding to words in $P(r+1,g-1)$, and by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Contains}, the maximal tori with respect to containment correspond to words with $\# \{ j \mid s_j = \epsilon \} = g-2-r$.  Each such word is obtained by choosing a subset of $[g-1]$ of size $g-2-r$ to fill with $\epsilon$'s, and filling the remaining entries with one of the two alternating substrings of length $r+1$.  It follows that the number of maximal tori in this union is exactly $2 \cdot {{g-1}\choose{g-2-r}}$.

Now, $V^1 (\Gamma,\pi)$ is a union of translates of the $g-1$ codimension-1 coordinate tori.  Each maximal torus $T(Q)$ therefore intersects $g-2-r$ general translates of $V^1 (\Gamma,\pi)$ in $(g-2-r)!$ points.  It follows that the intersection of $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ with these translates has cardinality
\[
2 \cdot {{g-1}\choose{g-2-r}} \cdot (g-2-r)! = 2 \cdot \frac{(g-1)!}{(r+1)!}.
\]

These translates can be chosen to contain a particular point $[D] \in V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ if $[D]$ lies in exactly one maximal torus $T(Q)$, which holds if $[D]$ is vertex avoiding.
head: environment

label: Prop:LCI
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop:LCI}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops and $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution.  Let $r \geq2$ and let $[D] \in V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$ be vertex avoiding.  There exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $[D]$ and effective divisors $E_1 , \ldots , E_{r+1}$ of degree $r-1$ such that
\[
V^r (\Gamma,\pi) \cap U = \Big( \bigcap_{i=1}^{r+1} V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + E_i - \iota^* E_i \Big) \cap U .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $[D'] \in P^r (\Gamma,\pi)$, and let $D' \in \vert D' \vert$ be its orientable representative.  Let $i \in [g-1]$ and let $p_i$ be a general point on the $i$th loop.  The key to this argument is to compute the orientable representative of $[D' - p_i + \iota^* p_i]$.  There are 4 cases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item  If $r$ is even, then the orientable representative of $[D' - p_i + \iota^* p_i]$ has a chip on the same point of the $j$th loop as $D'$ for all $j > i$, and a chip on the antipodal point of the $j$th loop from $D'$ for all $j<i$.  
\item  If $r$ is odd, then the orientable representative of $[D' - p_i + \iota^* p_i]$ has a chip on the same point of the $j$th loop as $D'$ for all $j < i$, and a chip on the antipodal point of the $j$th loop from $D'$ for all $j>i$.
\item  If $r$ is even, then the orientable representative of $[D' + p_i - \iota^* p_i]$ has a chip on the same point of the $j$th loop as $D'$ for all $j < i$, and a chip on the antipodal point of the $j$th loop from $D'$ for all $j>i$.  
\item  If $r$ is odd, then the orientable representative of $[D' + p_i - \iota^* p_i]$ has a chip on the same point of the $j$th loop as $D'$ for all $j > i$, and a chip on the antipodal point of the $j$th loop from $D'$ for all $j<i$.
\end{enumerate}

Now, let $Q = s_1 \cdots s_{g-1} \in P(r+1,g-1)$ and let $A = \{ i \in [g-1] \mid s_i \neq \epsilon \}$.  Suppose that $\# A = r+1$ and $[D] \in T(Q)$.  For $i \in A$, let $i'$ be either the largest element of $A$ that is smaller than $i$, or the smallest element of $A$ that is larger than $i$.  (Since $\# A \geq 2$, there always exists an element $i' \in A$ that is not equal to $i$.)  Now, partition $A \smallsetminus \{ i,i' \}$ into sets $B_i$ and $B'_i$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item  if $r$ is even and the orientable representative $D$ of $[D]$ has a chip at $v_i$, or $r$ is odd and $D$ has a chip at $w_i$, then $\# \{ b \in B_i \mid b < i,i' \}$ is equal to either $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b < i,i' \}$ or $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b < i,i' \} + 1$ and $\# \{ b \in B_i \mid b > i,i' \}$ is equal to either $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b > i,i' \}$ or $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b > i,i' \} - 1$. 
\item  if $r$ is even and $D$ has a chip at $w_i$, or $r$ is odd and $D$ has a chip at $v_i$, then $\# \{ b \in B_i \mid b < i,i' \}$ is equal to either $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b < i,i' \}$ or $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b < i,i' \} - 1$ and $\# \{ b \in B_i \mid b > i,i' \}$ is equal to either $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b > i,i' \}$ or $\# \{ b \in B'_i \mid b > i,i' \} + 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Let
\[
E_i = \sum_{j \in B_i} p_j + \sum_{j \in B'_i} \iota^* p_j .
\]
Our goal is to show that
\[
V^r (\Gamma,\pi) \cap U = \Big( \bigcap_{i=1}^{r+1} V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + E_i - \overline{E}_i \Big) \cap U .
\]
By the definition of rank, the lefthand side is contained in the righthand side.  It therefore suffices to show the reverse containment.

Let $[D'] \in (V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + E_i - \iota^* E_i) \cap U$, and let $D'_i$ be the orientable representative of $[D' - E_i + \iota^* E_i]$.  Since $[D'] \in U$ and $U$ is sufficiently small, it follows by induction, using (1)-(4) above, that $D'_i$ has a chip in a small neighborhood of $v_i$, and this chip is at $v_i$ if and only if $D'$ has a chip on the same point of the $i$th loop as $D$.  Similarly, $D'_i$ has a chip in a small neighborhood of $w_{i'}$, and a chip on the $j$th loop at a point distinct from $v_j$ or $w_j$ for all $j \notin \{ i,i' \}$.  By \cite[Lemma~3.5]{PBN}, since $D'_i$ has rank at least one, there exists $j \in [g-1]$ such that $D'_i$  has a chip at $v_j$.  By the above, we see that $j$ must be equal to $i$, hence $D'$ has a chip on the same point of the $i$th loop as $D$.  

Now, if $[D'] \in \cap_{i=1}^{r+1} (V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + E_i - \iota^* E_i) \cap U$, it follows that $D'$ has a chip on the same point of the $i$th loop as $D$ for all $i$ such that $s_i \neq \epsilon$.  In other words, $[D'] \in T(Q)$, and the result follows.

label: Lem:Nonvacuous
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Nonvacuous}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops of genus $g$ and $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution.  Then there exists a bielliptic curve $C$ of genus $g$ and an \'{e}tale double cover $f \colon \widetilde{C} \to C$ specializing to $\pi$.  Moreover, the diagram \eqref{eq:tropical} lifts to the diagram \eqref{eq:classical}.  In particular, $g (C_1) = 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If the residue field has odd characteristic or characteristic zero, then by \cite[Lemma~7.15]{ABBR15a}, there is a map of smooth curves $p \colon C \to E$ specializing to $\psi$, where $C$ has genus $g$ and $E$ has genus 1.  By \cite[Lemma~5.9]{JensenLen18}, there exists a unique \'{e}tale double cover $f \colon \widetilde{C} \to C$ specializing to $\pi$.

We show that the cover $p \circ f \colon \widetilde{C} \to E$ is Galois.  Let $\tau \colon C \to C$ be the involution that transposes the sheets of the cover $p \colon C \to E$, and let $\eta \in \operatorname{Jac}_2 (C)$ be the unique nontrivial 2-torsion divisor in the kernel of $f^*$.  By \cite[Corollary~4.3]{Naranjo}, the cover is Galois if and only if $\tau^* (\eta) = \eta$.  The involution $\tau$ specializes to the involution of $\Gamma$ that transposes the sheets of the cover $\psi $.  Composing this involution with the cover $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ produces an isomorphic double cover.  Since the double cover lifts uniquely, it follows that $\tau^* (\eta) = \eta$.

Since the cover $p \circ f \colon \widetilde{C} \to E$ is Galois, by \cite{Debarre} the Galois group must be the Klein-4 subgroup of $S_4$ that acts on the 4 sheets by products of 2 disjoint transpositions.  Each of these involutions specializes to an involution of $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ that acts on the sheets in the same way.  In other words, the involutions $\iota , \iota_1$, and $\iota_2$ are specializations of involutions on $\widetilde{C}$.   Thus, the diagram \eqref{eq:tropical} lifts to the diagram \eqref{eq:classical}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The case where $r=1$ is proven in \cite[Lemma~5.1]{PBN}, so we assume that $r \geq 2$.  The tropicalization of the Prym-Brill-Noether variety $V^r (C,f)$ is a closed subset of $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$, and the set of vertex avoiding divisor classes is dense in $V^r (\Gamma,\pi)$, so it suffices to consider the case where $[D]$ is vertex avoiding.  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:TropIntersection}, there exist divisors $D_1 , \ldots , D_{g-2-r} \in P^r (\Gamma,\pi) - P^1 (\Gamma,\pi)$ such that
\[
X = \bigcap_{i=1}^{g-2-r} [V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + D_i ] \cap V^r (\Gamma,\pi)
\]
is finite, contains $[D]$, and
\[
\# X = 2 \cdot \frac{(g-1)!}{(r+1)!}.
\]

Let $\mathcal{D}_i \in P^r (C,f) - P^1 (C,f)$ be a divisor on $C$ such that $\operatorname{Trop} (\mathcal{D}_i) = D_i$, and let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \operatorname{Pic} (\widetilde{C})$ be
\[
\mathcal{X} = \bigcap_{i=1}^{g-2-r} [V^1 (C,f) + \mathcal{D}_i ] \cap V^r (C,f).
\]
Since $\operatorname{Trop} (\mathcal{X}) \subseteq X$, we see that $\mathcal{X}$ is finite, and $g(C_1) = 1$ by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Nonvacuous}.  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Intersection}, we have
\[
\# \mathcal{X} \geq 2 \cdot \frac{(g-1)!}{(r+1)!}.
\]

By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LCI}, there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $[D]$ and effective divisors $E_1 , \ldots , E_{r+1}$ of degree $r-1$ such that
\[
V^r (\Gamma,\pi) \cap U = \Big( \bigcap_{i=1}^{r+1} V^1 (\Gamma,\pi) + E_i - \iota^*E_i \Big) \cap U .
\]
Let $\mathcal{E}_i$ be an effective divisor on $C$ such that $\operatorname{Trop} (\mathcal{E}_i) = E_i$.  By \cite[Proposition~5.4]{PBN}, the Prym-Brill-Noether variety $V^r (C,f)$ is contained in $\cap_{i=1}^{r+1} (V^1 (C,f) + \mathcal{E}_i - \iota^* \mathcal{E}_i)$.

In the open set $U$, the hypersurfaces $\operatorname{Trop} (V^1 (C,f)) + D_i$ and $\operatorname{Trop} (V^1 (C,f) + E_i - \iota^* E_i$ are translates of coordinate tori, and each has multiplicity one by \cite[Lemma~5.1]{PBN}.  By \cite{Rabinoff12}, it follows that there is at most one point tropicalizing to $[D]$ in the intersection of these $g-1$ hypersurfaces.  In other words, the tropicalization map $\operatorname{Trop} \colon \mathcal{X} \to X$ is injective.  But since $\# \mathcal{X} \geq \# X$, it must in fact be bijective.

label: Cor:Reduced
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor:Reduced}
Let $\Gamma$ be a bielliptic loop of loops of genus $g$ and $\pi \colon \widetilde{\Gamma} \to \Gamma$ the quotient by the antipodal involution.  If $f \colon \widetilde{C} \to C$ is an \'{e}tale double cover of smooth curves specializing to $\pi$ with $C$ bielliptic, then $V^r (C,f)$ is reduced.  In particular, if $g-1 = r+1$, then $V^r (C,f)$ is smooth.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proof of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Lifting} demonstrates that the intersection of $V^r (C,f)$ with $r+1$ general translates of $V^1 (C,f)$ consists of distinct reduced points.  Thus, $V^r (C,f)$ is smooth at these points.  Since $V^r (C,f)$ is Cohen-Macualuay, it has no embedded points, hence it is reduced.

label: Cor:Class
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor:Class}
Let $r \geq 2$.  For a general \'{e}tale double cover $f \colon C \to \widetilde{C} \in \mathcal{R}_{B,g,0}$, one has the following equality of cohomology classes:
\[
[ V^r (C,f) ] =  2 \cdot \frac{\Theta^{r+1}}{(r+1)!} .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Intersection}, there exists an integer $m_r \geq 2$ such that
\[
[ V^r (C,f) ] =  m_r \cdot \frac{\Theta^{r+1}}{(r+1)!} .
\]
Moreover, there exist divisors $D_1 , \ldots , D_{g-r-2} \in P^r (C,f) - P^1 (C,f)$ such that
\[
\mathcal{X} = \bigcap_{i=1}^{g-r-2} [V^1 (C,f) + D_i ] \cap V^r (C,f)
\]
is finite.  The proof of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Lifting} demonstrates that $\mathcal{X}$ consists of exactly $2 \cdot \frac{(g-1)!}{(r+1)!}$ points, and by Corollary~\ref{Cor:Class}, this intersection is reduced.  It follows that $m_r = 2$.
